Chapter 14 sends him through a fall and an underwater sequence, which echoes the old myth pattern of death and rebirth and gives students concrete proof of his divine parentage.","enduringUnderstanding":"Writers retell ancient story patterns in modern settings, and a single turning-point episode can reveal a hero's identity and raise the stakes of a quest.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 22, students read Chapter 15 and analyze how the novel references the myth of Ares and Aphrodite. Tonight's homework previews that myth and Chapter 15.","performanceTask":"Shared Stories, Shared Lessons asks students to explain how a key event functions as a turning point. to touch gently","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"onlookers","definition":"people who watch something happen without taking part","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"surveillance","definition":"close watching of a person or place, often to gather information","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"turning point","definition":"a moment in a story when something important changes and the direction of the plot shifts","tier":"support"},{"word":"divine","definition":"having to do with a god","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Book 1)","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapter 14, pp. 212–217 (vocabulary pages); homework pp. 219–233"},{"title":"Excerpt from “The Song of Ares and Aphrodite”","pages":"Homework"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate their knowledge of old myths and of the hero's journey, and get ready to look for a death-and-rebirth pattern in Chapter 14.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"Dying and Coming Back","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.5"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn and talk with a partner. Think of a story, myth, or movie where a hero seems to be defeated, goes down into a dark place, and then comes back stronger. What happens to the hero when they return?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What stories do you know where a hero goes through something that feels like a death and then comes back changed?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In a lot of superhero movies the hero seems to lose and then comes back stronger. In the Greek myths, heroes go into the underworld and come back, like Hercules. When they come back they know more about who they are."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today we read Chapter 14, where Percy falls into a river after a fight. Watch for what the author keeps from the old pattern and what he makes modern. Ask yourself what the chapter reveals about who Percy really is."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to 5 minutes. Accept any hero story, including video games and films. You are only priming the idea of going down, near-death, and returning changed."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students learn Chapter 14 vocabulary in context, add the words to their Unit Vocabulary graphic organizers, and practice fluency with a passage that includes a target word.","activities":[{"id":"lab-vocab-in-context","title":"Chapter 14 Vocabulary in Context","minutes":6,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.6","RL.6.4"],"routine":"Introduce New Words in Context","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 14","pages":"pp. 212–217"},{"type":"directions","text":"Find each word in the chapter on the page shown: fugitive, revelation, mortality (p. 212); sonar (p. 214); foul, descend, immune, caress (p. 215); onlookers (p. 216); surveillance (p. 217). Read the sentence around the word, make a guess about its meaning, and add the word to your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let's start with the three words on page 212. Read the sentence with *fugitive*. Percy and his friends are running and hiding. A fugitive is a person who is running away, often from danger or the law. *Revelation* is a surprising truth that is suddenly made known. *Mortality* means being human and certain to die someday. Notice that *mortality* comes from the same root as *mortal*, a word we use for humans in the myths."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why might a fugitive on a quest be thinking about mortality?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy is being chased and he could really die. A fugitive is in danger, so he has to think about the fact that he's mortal and can be hurt."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Now the water words. On page 214, *sonar* is a system that uses sound to find things underwater. On page 215, *foul* means dirty and unpleasant, *descend* means to go down, *immune* means protected so something can't harm you, and *caress* is a gentle touch. On page 216, *onlookers* are people who watch without joining in. On page 217, *surveillance* is careful watching of a person or place."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"The river water is foul, but the text uses a word like *caress* to describe how it feels to Percy. Why is that surprising?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Foul water should feel gross or dangerous, but a caress is gentle. That shows the water doesn't hurt Percy and might even feel friendly to him, which is a clue that he's the son of the sea god."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Point students to pages rather than reading all the sentences aloud. If a word is hard to find, give the paragraph's first few words. The caress question previews tonight's evidence about Percy's powers, so let it stay short."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners connect new words to context and to words they know.","sayAsk":"Say: Point to the word on the page and read the sentence with your partner. Ask: What clue in the sentence helps you? Frames: I think ___ means ___ because the sentence says ___. ___ is like ___ in my language. Invite students to link cognates such as revelation/revelación, mortality/mortalidad, descend/descender, and surveillance/vigilancia where they exist.","watchFor":"If students guess without using the sentence, then prompt: Which words near the word give you a clue? If students define a word with a synonym only, then ask them to use it in a sentence about Percy. Success: students use a context clue to explain a word's meaning."}]},{"id":"lab-fluency-routine","title":"Fluency Routine: Partner Read","minutes":4,"standards":["RL.6.10","L.6.6"],"routine":"Partner Fluency Practice","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 14","pages":"p. 215 (passage with descend, immune, foul, and caress)"},{"type":"directions","text":"Partner A reads the passage on page 215 aloud, then Partner B reads it. Read for accuracy and expression. When you reach a vocabulary word, read it clearly and say it with the right feeling. Then talk for 30 seconds about which words helped you picture the scene."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"First read for accuracy, then for expression. Let your voice show the shift from fear to calm as Percy sinks. Listen to your partner and give one compliment and one tip."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which vocabulary word was the most important for understanding how Percy feels underwater?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think *immune* because it shows that the water can't hurt him. Nothing bad happens to Percy even though he's at the bottom of a river."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and listen for students who skip or stumble on target words. Have them reread the sentence once. Remind students to finish adding all ten words to their organizers if they haven't yet."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: reading the vocabulary words fluently","tryTHis":"x","tryThis":"Echo-read the passage in small chunks, then have the student read the chunk back. Underline syllables in descend and surveillance before the first read."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: using vocabulary precisely","tryThis":"Ask students to write one original sentence about Percy that uses two target words, such as immune and descend, and explain how the pair of words shows his powers."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students cite concrete details from Chapter 14 as evidence of Percy's divine parentage and growing powers (RL.6.1). Part B: Students analyze how the fall, underwater sequence, and emergence form a turning point and how the chapter fits the hero's journey and raises the stakes (RL.6.5).","activities":[{"id":"lia-evidence-powers","title":"Part A: Evidence of Percy's Powers","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.1"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 14","pages":"pp. 212–217"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Strong evidence is concrete. It is not \"Percy is special.\" It is a specific detail you can point to on the page, such as what he does, what he doesn't feel, or what happens around him. Then we explain what that detail shows, whether it is stated directly or something we infer."},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread the fall into the river and the underwater sequence. Annotate the details that show Percy has powers: underline details about staying dry, circle details about breathing underwater, and star the moment he lights the lighter at the bottom of the river. In a two-column chart, write the detail (with page number) on the left and what it shows on the right. Mark each as stated or inferred."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What happens to Percy's body and clothes underwater, and what does that suggest?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On pages 215–216 Percy stays dry even though he's at the bottom of a river. A normal person would be soaked and sinking, so this suggests that the water obeys him because Poseidon is his father."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does it mean that Percy can breathe underwater and light a lighter at the bottom of the river?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Breathing underwater and keeping a flame lit are things that are impossible for a mortal. The author uses those details to prove Percy has a god's power over water. The text doesn't say it outright, so I inferred it from the details."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the word *immune* on page 215 help support your evidence?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It tells me the river can't hurt him. The author chose *immune* to show that the water has no effect on Percy, so it works as direct evidence that he's protected as Poseidon's son."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Listen for students who say Percy is just lucky. Redirect with: What is the pattern across the staying dry, breathing, and the lighter? One detail could be luck, but three details point to his parentage. Make sure each student cites a page number."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"Which detail from Chapter 14 is the strongest evidence of Percy's divine parentage?","choices":[{"text":"Percy is afraid when he is chased to the river.","correct":false,"rationale":"Fear is a normal human reaction and doesn't prove anything about his parentage. It is a believable but weak choice."},{"text":"Percy stays dry and breathes underwater at the bottom of the river, and even lights a lighter there.","correct":true,"rationale":"These concrete details are impossible for a mortal and show his control over water, which points to his father, Poseidon."},{"text":"The river water is described as foul.","correct":false,"rationale":"Foul describes how the water looks or smells. It doesn't show Percy's powers, and the text pairs it with the water's gentle effect on him."},{"text":"Onlookers watch Percy come out of the river.","correct":false,"rationale":"The onlookers show how others react to the scene, but they are not evidence of Percy's powers on their own."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in citing concrete details and explaining what they show, using adverbials to add details about time, place, and manner.","sayAsk":"Say: Show me the detail on the page. Ask: What does this detail show about Percy? Frames: On page ___, Percy ___ underwater, which shows ___. At the bottom of the river, Percy calmly ___. Suddenly, ___. Model expanding a sentence: Percy breathes. → Percy breathes easily at the bottom of the river. Have partners rehearse aloud before writing.","watchFor":"If students copy a long quotation without explaining it, then prompt: What does this show about Percy? If students give a short sentence, then ask: Where? When? How? to add an adverbial. Success: students pair a page-numbered detail with a clear explanation and use at least one adverbial phrase."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing concrete details over general statements","tryThis":"Give a sentence starter: On page ___, Percy ___. Have the student point to the exact line, then ask What would a normal person experience here? to highlight the contrast."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: stated versus inferred evidence","tryThis":"Ask students to find one inference about Percy's powers that no character says aloud, and explain which two details together lead to it."}]}]},{"id":"lia-turning-point","title":"Part B: Chapter 14 as a Turning Point","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.5","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 14","pages":"pp. 212–217"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A chapter can function like a turning point, a moment when the direction of the story changes. In a hero's journey, the hero often goes through a kind of death and rebirth: a fall into danger, a time in a dark place, and an emergence that leaves them changed. Today's question asks how this old pattern is retold in a modern way. In Chapter 14, the river replaces the underworld, and a lighter replaces a torch."},{"type":"directions","text":"Make a three-box sequence chart: The Fall, Underwater, Emergence. In each box, write one concrete detail from the chapter with its page number and what changes for Percy in that part. Then, in a Think-Pair-Share, answer the question below."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do the fall, the underwater sequence, and the emergence work together as a death-and-rebirth pattern?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The fall is like Percy dying because he plunges into danger and seems lost. Underwater is the dark place where he discovers his powers. When he comes out, he's like he was reborn because he knows he can control water and the people watching, the onlookers, see it too."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does this modern version emphasize that older myths might not?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It emphasizes Percy's identity. He doesn't descend to meet the dead like old heroes; he descends and learns he's the son of Poseidon. The modern setting, with a river, a lighter, and surveillance, makes it feel real."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does Chapter 14 fit into the whole structure of the book and raise the stakes of the quest?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"This chapter is a turning point because before it, Percy wasn't sure of his powers. After it, he's more confident, but he's also a bigger target as a fugitive. The stakes are higher because now others can see what he can do, and the quest feels more dangerous."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"If students struggle with structure language, return to the beginning-middle-end of the episode, then connect to the whole book: before the chapter, after the chapter, and what is different. Remind students to name what changes, not just what happens."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Now write two or three sentences that explain how Chapter 14 acts as a turning point. Use a time or place phrase such as *at the bottom of the river* or *after he emerges*, and cite one detail with a page number."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining sequence and structure with precise language and in expanding sentences with adverbials.","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner what happens first, next, and last in the episode. Ask: What changes after Percy comes out of the river? Frames: First, Percy ___. Underwater, he ___. After he emerges, he ___. This chapter is a turning point because ___. This raises the stakes by ___. Encourage students to rehearse in a home language first, then restate in English.","watchFor":"If students retell the whole chapter, then prompt: Which part changes Percy's situation most? If students list events without explaining change, then ask: What is different afterward? Success: students use sequence words and adverbials, and explain why the chapter is a turning point."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: explaining how a chapter fits the overall structure","tryThis":"Give a three-part frame: Before this chapter, Percy ___. In this chapter, he ___. After, he ___. Have the student fill it in orally first."},{"type":"support-table-placeholder","situation":"","tryThis":""}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students explain Chapter 14 as a turning point and connect the skill to the Performance Task.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-reflection","title":"Exit Ticket: Turning Point","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.5","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"In the Performance Task, you will explain how a key event functions as a turning point. Today you practiced by showing how Percy's fall into the river changes the quest."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the paragraph: Chapter 14 is a turning point in *The Lightning Thief* because ___. A key detail is that ___ (p. ___). This detail shows ___, and it raises the stakes of the quest because ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Chapter 14 is a turning point in *The Lightning Thief* because Percy learns how powerful he really is. A key detail is that he stays dry and breathes underwater (p. 215). This detail shows he is Poseidon's son, and it raises the stakes of the quest because now more people know who he is, so he is in more danger."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (Optional)","purpose":"Students read ahead to prepare for Lesson 22 and its connection to a Greek myth.","activities":[{"id":"homework-ch15-and-myth","title":"Read Chapter 15 and the Myth Excerpt","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"1) Read the summary of Chapter 15 (pp. 219 to the top of p. 224, ending with \"Come on, let's find some dinner.\"). 2) Read and annotate Chapter 15 of *The Lightning Thief* (p. 224, starting \"A few minutes later,\" to p. 233). 3) Read and annotate the excerpt from \"The Song of Ares and Aphrodite.\" As you annotate, mark one detail about how the gods behave and one detail that seems to connect to a myth you know."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students analyze Chapter 14 of The Lightning Thief, citing concrete details such as Percy staying dry, breathing underwater, and lighting a lighter at the bottom of the river as evidence of his divine parentage.
